prize_parts.citation: for the invention and development of optical lattice clocks, which brought atomic timekeeping to the 10^-18 level

statement.case_for: Optical lattice clocks are a clearly identifiable invention with lasting consequences. Katori's magic-wavelength idea removed Doppler, recoil and trap-shift limits by holding many neutral atoms in the Lamb-Dicke regime, and Ye's group then pushed accuracy and stability to the 10^-18 level and made inter-laboratory comparison routine. The method has been reproduced independently in several species and laboratories, it anchors the roadmap for redefining the second, and it enables relativistic geodesy and sensitive tests of fundamental constants. Five of the eight members ranked it, three of them first, and all five who ranked it proposed the same two names, which is rare on this shortlist. In my opening ballot I placed circuit QED first, but on reflection I am not the right person to carry that case. Circuit QED is my own research area, it sits next to the 2025 award on macroscopic quantum effects in circuits, and the four-name credit list cannot be reduced to three without leaving a major theorist out. The clock case is mature, attributable to two people, and does not depend on my home field.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is that the committee has already honoured the frequency comb in 2005 and trapped-ion control in 2012, so lattice clocks may look like an incremental step in a lineage that has been rewarded twice. Priority for the first Sr lattice-clock demonstrations is also shared with Takamoto, Ido and others, and Lemonde's group made comparable contributions. Finally, Ye's name is tied as much to comb and laser stabilisation as to the lattice clock, and the redefinition of the second is still pending, so the story is not yet finished.

responses.point: Kroll ranks optical lattice clocks first: a clean two-person credit, with Katori's magic-wavelength proposal and Ye's record accuracy, and a natural successor to the 2005 and 2012 clock-related prizes.
responses.response: I agree on the structure of the credit and have moved the clocks above my own field in my preferred configuration. Where I would qualify his view is the argument that the 2005 and 2012 prizes make the timing natural. The same history can be read as saying the lineage is already well honoured. We should therefore frame the citation around the lattice-trapping architecture and its 10^-18 performance, not around clocks in general, so that the novelty relative to comb and ion work is explicit in the text.

responses.point: Lindroth ranks lattice clocks first and notes unresolved credit for Lemonde and others, with a possible overlap with the thorium nuclear clock and with earlier ion-clock work.
responses.response: Her priority concern is fair, and I do not think the supplied evidence settles it. Takamoto, Ido and Lemonde contributed to the first lattice-clock measurements and to the cross-checks, and a two-person prize leaves them out. I still consider Katori the clear originator of the concept, and Ye the person who made it the record-setting standard. A two-name award is defensible if the citation is written around the concept and its performance. On thorium, I would keep it out of this discussion because it is a separate and still developing result.

responses.point: Danielsson ranks the experimental Higgs discovery first as a decisive, timely completion of the Standard Model, with the founding leaders of ATLAS and CMS as the credited names.
responses.response: I ranked the Higgs discovery last on my own ballot because it is outside my expertise and I defer to colleagues on the physics, but I disagree with his attribution argument. The 2013 prize already honoured the idea, and what remains is an experiment with thousands of authors. A prize for Della Negra, Jenni and Virdee would be rewarding organisational leadership as a stand-in for discovery, and the analysis and detector decisions that produced the signal are spread across many people. I accept that the achievement is of the highest importance, but I do not yet see a defensible, short, individual credit, and I would want to hear what concretely each of the three contributed to the observation.

responses.point: Eriksson ranks room-temperature tunnel magnetoresistance first and the topological insulator candidate third, and observes that the topological-insulator credit omits Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang and the 3D discoverers.
responses.response: I share his concern about the topological-insulator credit, and it is the reason I keep that case as an alternative and not my preferred option. Kane and Mele are decisive on the Z2 classification, but the HgTe experiment followed the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang proposal, and the 3D extension is credited to others, so the trio would leave out contributors who are hard to rank below Molenkamp. The 2016 topological-phases award adds a second difficulty. I find tunnel magnetoresistance technically strong but have not ranked it, and I would like to hear how he weighs the Yuasa and Djayaprawira contribution to the MgO step against the three supplied names.

uncertainties: Whether lattice clocks are seen as distinct enough from the 2005 comb and 2012 ion-control prizes.
Fair treatment of Takamoto, Ido and Lemonde in a two-person credit.
Whether my own downgrade of circuit QED is justified, or whether the committee should hear the case from a member without a connection to the field.
Whether a close follow-on to the 2025 circuit prize is a concern for either circuit QED or other quantum-technology candidates.
statement.conflict_note: I work in circuit and waveguide QED, direct WACQT at Chalmers, and have close Chalmers links to Per Delsing and C. M. Wilson and frequent collaboration with Anton Frisk Kockum, so I should disclose a connection to the circuit QED candidate (B033) and would consider recusal from the final decision on it. I also note that Chalmers hosted researchers associated with the 2025 prize. No specific conflict is apparent from my profile for the optical lattice clock candidate.
